title: Amutrabhūyāt: freed from Yama’s claim
theme: Bṛhaspati is praised for freeing the speaker from Yama’s claim and from disgrace, and Agni is told that the Aśvins, physicians of the gods, have pushed death away.

words.meaning: from being in the yonder world
words.context: The commentator, reading a change of case (vyatyaya), takes it as an instrumental: «अमुत्रभवेन परलोकभवेन सुखेन मां संयोजयेति शेषः» — join me with the happiness of the other world.
The anonymous commentator: «एतद्द्वयान्मोचयित्वाऽथानन्तरम्» — having freed [me] from these two, then
The anonymous commentator: he supplies fear: «यमस्य संबन्धि यद्भयं» — the fear that belongs to Yama
The anonymous commentator: Bṛhaspati is «बृहतां वेदवाचां पतिः», the lord of the great words of the Veda; he takes it as an address to the supreme self
The anonymous commentator: «अभिशस्तेरपयशसोऽपि माममुञ्चः» — from disgrace too you freed me

words.role: main verb of the first line
words.context: The anonymous commentator: read as a request: «तस्मान्माममुञ्चो मोचय» — free me from that
The anonymous commentator: as a wish: «मृत्युं प्रत्यौहतां दूरी कुर्वाताम्» — may they put death far off
The anonymous commentator: «देववैद्यावस्मान्मत्तः सकाशान्मृत्युं प्रत्यौहतां दूरी कुर्वाताम्» — the two physicians of the gods

words.gram: m. nom. du. (Vedic -ā), or instr. sg.
words.meaning: the two physicians; or, by the physician
words.context: The anonymous commentator: he takes it as an instrumental agreeing with Agni: «हेऽग्ने देवानां संबन्धिना भिषजा»
The anonymous commentator: «शचीभिरिन्द्रपत्नीभिः संयोजयेत्यपि शेषः» — he reads Śacī, Indra’s consort, in the plural: join me with them as well

sandhi.type: t before a vowel and before y
sandhi.rule: amutrabhūyāt + adha → amutrabhūyād adha; yat + yamasya → yad yamasya (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).

sandhi.type: visarga after e before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The visarga of abhiśasteḥ becomes r before a vowel.

sandhi.type: m before a vowel; t before d
sandhi.rule: mṛtyum asmat join unchanged; asmat + devānām → asmad devānām (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).

sandhi_exceptions.note: bṛhaspate · abhiśasteḥ: the e of the vocative kept before a without elision (classical bṛhaspate ’bhiśasteḥ); a Vedic hiatus (prakṛtibhāva, P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे)), printed so in every witness.

morphology.note: The Vedic dual in -ā for -au (P. 7.1.39 (सुपां सुलुक्पूर्वसवर्णाऽऽच्छेयाडाड्यायाजालः)); the commentator glosses it aśvinau.
An augmented past of √ūh ‘to push’ (a + ūh → auh); with prati, ‘they pushed back’. The commentator renders it as a wish.

translation.literal: From being in the yonder world, then, from what is Yama’s, O Bṛhaspati, from curse you freed [me]. The two Aśvins pushed death back from us, the two physicians of the gods, O Agni, with their powers.
translation.readable: Bṛhaspati, you set me free from going to the other world, from what belongs to Yama, and from disgrace. Agni, the two Aśvins, physicians of the gods, drove death away from us by their skill.

anvaya: बृहस्पते [त्वम्] अमुत्रभूयात् यत् यमस्य [तस्मात्] अध अभिशस्तेः [माम्] अमुञ्चः । अग्ने देवानाम् भिषजा अश्विना शचीभिः मृत्युम् अस्मत् प्रति औहताम् ।
syntax: Two sentences, each addressed to a god: Bṛhaspati, with the verb amuñcaḥ and three ablatives of what one is freed from; Agni, with the Aśvins as subject of praty-auhatām, death as object and asmat as the ablative ‘from us’.

ambiguities.note: The verbs are past (amuñcaḥ, auhatām): the verse states what the gods have done. The commentator renders both as requests (mocaya, dūrī kurvātām).

A dual, ‘the two physicians of the gods’, in apposition to the Aśvins; or, as the commentator takes it, an instrumental singular describing Agni, ‘by you, the physician of the gods’. He explains Agni as physician because, carrying the oblations, he takes away the gods’ hunger («हविर्नयनद्वारा देवताक्षुन्निवारकत्वादग्नेर्भिषक्त्वं द्रष्टव्यम्»).
In Vedic usage ‘with powers, with skill’; the commentator reads Śacī, Indra’s consort, in the plural.
An ablative, ‘from being in the other world’, that is, from death; the commentator, by a change of case, reads ‘with the happiness of the other world’.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: One triṣṭubh verse printed in two lines of 22 syllables.

beginner: This verse speaks to two gods. First it thanks Bṛhaspati, the lord of sacred speech, for having set the speaker free from going to the other world, from what belongs to Yama, the ruler of the dead, and from disgrace. Then it turns to Agni, the fire, and says that the two Aśvins, the twin physicians of the gods, have pushed death away from us. The old commentator reads these past tenses as requests: free me, push death away. He also reads one word as describing Agni himself as the gods’ physician, because by carrying offerings to them Agni takes away their hunger. Like the verses before it, this one asks that death keep its distance.
analogy: Like thanking a friend for a past rescue while asking for the same help again.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That Bṛhaspati freed the speaker from the other world, from what is Yama’s and from disgrace, and that the Aśvins, physicians of the gods, pushed death away.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: Bṛhaspati, the lord of the Veda’s great words, is the supreme self; the speaker asks to be freed from the fear that belongs to Yama («यमस्य संबन्धि यद्भयं तस्मान्माममुञ्चो मोचय») and from disgrace, and then to be joined with the happiness of the other world.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: because, by carrying the oblations, Agni removes the hunger of the gods («हविर्नयनद्वारा देवताक्षुन्निवारकत्वादग्नेर्भिषक्त्वं द्रष्टव्यम्»).

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse remembers help already given before it asks again. Recalling what has already carried us through can steady us when we need help once more. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who has helped you through a hard time?
reflect.deeper: Why might the verse put its requests in the past tense, as things already done?
reflect.practice: Thank one person this week for help they gave you long ago.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).
The same verse opens Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 7.53. The edition does not import Atharvaveda passages, so its wording is not checked here.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text lacks शचीभिः here (corrections.json, review): it prints the word after the verse number, at the start of 10.49 (logged there as a witness error). The word belongs to this verse; the base and the Ānandāśrama text agree, and the commentator explains it here.
The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text reads मृत्यमस्माद्देवानाम् (corrections.json, witness errors); the base and the Tirupati e-text read मृत्युमस्मद्देवानाम्.
